```{r}
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey55") + geom_point(alpha = .35, size = .7) +
    facet_wrap(~model_id, scales = "free", ncol = 2) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    labs(x = "Conditional fitted response (m or m/year)", y = "Conditional Pearson residual",
      title = "RD03 exploratory model diagnostics")
  ggsave(file.path(p2, "figures/residual-review.png"), diag_plot, width = 9, height = 9, dpi = 160, bg = "white")
  p2_write(bind_rows(fit_records), "rd03-fit-register")
  writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), file.path(p2, "tables/session-info.txt"))
}
knitr::kable(p2_read("simulation-diagnostics"), digits = 5)
```

The grouped residual table checks for errors hidden by an overall diagnostic:
a model might fit one species, treatment, or period less well than the others.
Compare residual means, spread, and tails across those groups; simulation-scaled
residual means are expected to be near 0.5 under a well-matched model.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-grouped-residuals-review
knitr::kable(p2_read("grouped-residuals"), digits = 3)
```

The paired residual table checks whether the two increments from a clump still
move together after accounting for its fitted effects. This can flag remaining
dependence, but the fitted clump effects themselves influence these correlations;
the table cannot establish the underlying covariance or measurement error.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-paired-residuals-review
knitr::kable(p2_read("paired-residuals"), digits = 3)
```

The macro-plot residual table helps locate errors shared by many clumps in one
treatment unit. Such a pattern matters because many clumps with similar errors
are not independent evidence that a treatment response is estimated precisely.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-macro-residuals-review
knitr::kable(p2_read("macro-residuals"), digits = 3)
```

The residual plot complements the tables by showing curves, changing spread, or
extreme observations that averages can hide. We use it to decide which model
assumptions need closer review before accepting a display.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-residual-figure-review
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(p2, "figures/residual-review.png"))
```

Gaussian(log) year-10 simulations produce 0.47% nonpositive heights, versus
0.66% for the identity link and none for Gamma. Gamma nevertheless has poorer
AIC and a uniform-residual diagnostic p-value of 0.0015, so positive support
alone does not make it preferable. The separate temporal-macro increment
models generate roughly 1.25% nonpositive tanoak and 1.77% nonpositive redwood
increments, compared with none observed. Gaussian increments permit negative
changes in principle, but this lower-tail mismatch deserves targeted review.
The simulation diagnostics do not otherwise flag strong overall dispersion
or outlier departures; their nonsignificant p-values do not validate the models.
The residual figure also retains the larger positive increment tail. We retain
the family/support trade-off for Phase Three rather than claiming that any
candidate passes all scientific checks.

### Human review summary and Phase Three handoff {#rd03-phase-three}

**Phase Two is complete. I recommend the models below as the starting point for
Phase Three; none is yet accepted for the manuscript.** We used all 692 recorded
clumps, as approved in human review. Each treatment was represented at four
sites; the hundreds of clumps are subsamples within those treatment units.
Some blocks may have had too few clumps to reach the sampling target, but we
have no original roster to confirm that explanation. Our results describe this
recorded cohort and cannot establish survival or recruitment across the stand.

The model names identify the response and species: `h` means year-10 height,
`i` means annualized height change, `SESE` is redwood, and `LIDE` is tanoak.
Here, height always follows the tallest sprout on a clump at each visit; the
tallest stem may change between visits.

**Year-10 height:** the separate redwood model, `h_SESE`, estimates that GS clumps
were 4.65 m taller than HD clumps on average. Its estimate for HA minus HD is
only 0.96 m, with an approximate interval from -0.63 to +2.56 m. The joint model,
`h_diagonal`, gives almost the same two differences: 4.64 and 0.99 m. When we
refitted `h_diagonal` leaving out one site at a time, GS minus HD remained
positive, whereas HA minus HD ranged from 0.05 to 1.58 m. Thus GS versus HD is
the stronger result to carry forward. We should not yet claim a clear advantage
of aggregated retention (HA) over dispersed retention (HD).

**Change in growth rate:** `i_SESE_macro` models redwood separately and allows
each macro plot to have a different growth rate in each measurement period.
It estimates that annual height change was lower in years 5–10 than in years
1–5 by about 0.16, 0.16, 0.06, and 0.12 m/year under GS, LD, HA, and HD,
respectively. However, its intervals do not clearly distinguish how much slowing
occurred under GS versus HD or HA versus HD. The corresponding tanoak model,
`i_LIDE_macro`, also estimates slowing under every treatment, but each interval
includes no change. These two models fit better than `i_SESE` and `i_LIDE`,
which assume that a macro plot's contribution stays constant across periods.
**I recommend carrying `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` forward**, because that
constant contribution would cancel when comparing periods and leave out
variation among treatment units in how growth changed.

There is an important limit to those growth models. Both fit successfully using
all four sites and agree under two fitting algorithms. But three of their eight
site-omission fits had convergence problems: both species when Camp Six was
omitted, and redwood when Waldo South was omitted. Phase Three needs to examine
that instability before accepting their uncertainty intervals. We should not
remove those sites or treat the failed fits as reliable results.

**Residual redwood trees:** `rh_residual` compares year-10 redwood height between
clumps with and without a tree left after harvest, allowing for treatment and
site. It estimates about 5% greater height with a residual tree, but the interval
ranges from about 5% shorter to 16% taller. `ri_residual` makes the corresponding
growth-rate comparison and also leaves both suppression and augmentation
plausible. Neither model improves fit enough to justify adding the indicator
to the main analysis. **I recommend keeping these as secondary exploratory
results and leaving `residual_rw` out of the main treatment models.** This
comparison uses LD, HA, and HD only: GS has no residual trees. It does not
establish that retaining a tree causes either a benefit or a reduction in growth.

Use the following table as the Phase Three decision list: it names the models
we recommend carrying forward and the checks still needed before accepting
each one. This makes the next analysis choices explicit without treating the
current candidates as final selections.

| Question | Recommended Phase Three starting models | What to check before acceptance |
|---|---|---|
| Year-10 height | Start with `h_SESE` and `h_LIDE`: separate Gaussian(log) models with treatment, site, and macro-plot effects. Keep `h_diagonal` and `h_fixed` as joint-species comparisons. | Check simulated heights and uncertainty for each separate model. The related `h_diagonal` model generates about five nonpositive heights per 1,000 simulated measurements. `h_gamma` avoids this but fits the observed data less well. |
| Change in growth rate | Start with `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro`, which allow different amounts of slowing among treatments and macro plots. | Investigate the failed site-omission fits and calibrate uncertainty. Keep `i_full` as a comparison: it assumes one macro contribution across periods and shares clump variance across species. `i_diagonal` also forces equal slowing across treatments within a species. |
| Residual trees | Keep `rh_residual` and `ri_residual` as secondary checks against their matching models without the indicator, `rh_base` and `ri_base`. | Report the LD/HA/HD comparison and its uncertainty. Do not add the indicator to the main treatment models or expand the interaction search on this evidence. |

For all main comparisons, **I recommend averaging the four site predictions
equally when reporting treatment means**, rather than weighting them by the
number of clumps sampled. The current intervals are approximate; Phase Three
still needs to assess their reliability with only four sites.

The next analyst should proceed in this order:

1. Read this summary, the [candidate plan](#rd03-model-plan), and the numerical
   evidence above. Checkpoint the Phase Two sources and versioned outputs before
   further analytical changes. Run
   `python publication/scripts/check-analysis.py --inputs-only --protected` and
   `python publication/scripts/check-analysis.py --task RD03 --domains sprouts --require-models`.
   All 54 fits, including failed site omissions, have ignored RDS files under
   `outputs/sprouts/phase-two/models/`; the fit register records their status.
   Missing fits are prerequisites, not authority to silently refit.
2. Review the recommended models in the table before making a final selection.
   For `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro`, investigate why some three-site fits
   fail and explain any simpler model used in response. Retain variation among
   macro plots in the change between periods. Fit the planned joint-height
   sensitivity: one model of heights at years 1, 5, and 10, treating the visits
   as separate ages rather than assuming a straight growth line. Derive both
   interval changes from that model, so the shared year-5 measurement is handled
   within one analysis. It has **not** been fitted in Phase Two. A lognormal
   height model is also untested; add it only if reviewing simulated low heights
   and residuals gives a reason to do so. If added, include the likelihood
   Jacobian for comparison and the correction needed to report arithmetic means.
3. Review species/treatment/period and macro residual tables and the diagnostic
   figure, including the negative simulation fractions. Keep the observed-site
   arithmetic target consistent and do not compare AIC across endpoints or
   across different row subsets. Cross-species formal contrasts require a joint
   covariance model or paired hierarchical simulation; separate fits alone do
   not supply them. Do not expand the residual-tree search merely to find a
   favorable association.
4. Assess uncertainty by simulating new datasets from each chosen model and
   refitting it **2,000 times**, using seed **20261116**. This is the planned
   parametric bootstrap; it has **not** been run. Preserve
   the 16 macros, species, repeated clumps, observed site blocks, and fitted
   heterogeneity. Integrate log-link macro effects within every refit so that
   their variance uncertainty enters arithmetic means. Report failures,
   boundaries, Monte Carlo endpoint stability, and intervals' dependence on
   model assumptions. Use the four predeclared redwood contrasts with Holm
   adjustment if confirmatory testing is retained; other comparisons stay
   exploratory. This checks uncertainty under the chosen model's assumptions;
   it does not account for uncertainty about which model to choose or bias from
   how clumps were sampled.
5. Only after reviewing model adequacy and calibrated contrasts, prepare the
   proposed size/time figure and caption for acceptance. If treatment-specific
   temporal evidence remains weak, use an appropriately labeled pooled change
   or place temporal detail in the supplement. Refresh RD03, then its RT02,
   M02, and D02 review records from the registry. Those tasks remain queued;
   no manuscript claim or publication figure is accepted by this phase.

At the Phase Two handoff, an ordinary render read saved tables,
`-P recompute:true` rebuilt Phase Two summaries, and `-P refit:true` refitted
the Phase Two sequence. The Phase Three implementation below adds explicit
`-P refit_phase_three:true` for its new fits and `-P bootstrap:true` for its
2,000-dataset simulations. Recomputation otherwise requires their saved models
and bootstrap draws. No thesis environment, input export, package dependency,
or RD02 result changed.

Phase Two gives us named models to take forward and a clearer distinction
between the results they support. The year-10 GS–HD redwood height difference
is consistent across the tested models. HA–HD height differences and differences
among treatments in how much growth slowed need more cautious interpretation.
That handoff motivates the Phase Three analysis below, which assesses
uncertainty and prepares a display proposal for this recorded clump cohort.

## Phase Three: model adequacy and refitted uncertainty {#rd03-phase-three-analysis}

Do the recommended models give a dependable account of attained height and
changes in growth rate, despite only four treatment replicates? We carry forward
the separate Gaussian(log) year-10 models and the separate Gaussian increment
models with two correlated macro-period effects. Site predictions receive equal
weight. These models describe the recorded clumps, integrating macro effects
without extrapolating to an exchangeable population of sites. Residual-tree
associations remain the secondary Phase Two checks.

### Numerical investigation and a joint model of measured heights

We first check both year-10 models with BFGS and revisit all eight temporal
site omissions with that optimizer. A diagonal macro-period covariance is a
targeted sensitivity: it retains treatment-unit variation in period change but
sets the two macro effects' covariance to zero. It is not selected merely to
obtain convergence. Each saved fit records convergence, Hessian, gradients,
warnings, and covariance boundaries; failed fits supply no usable intervals.

The joint-height sensitivity uses categorical ages 1, 5, and 10, treatment by
age means, and site by age blocking. For each species, separate unstructured
three-age covariance matrices initially represent macros and clumps. If the
macro covariance is singular, a rank-two macro covariance provides the targeted
simplification, retaining age-specific loadings and macro variation in derived
increment changes. We retain the failed unrestricted fits in the register.
We set residual
dispersion to glmmTMB's near-zero value, so the clump matrix represents the
entire within-clump covariance; adding free residual scales would be
unidentifiable. This model handles the shared year-5 measurement without
assuming a growth curve or decomposing measurement error from clump variation.
It uses Gaussian identity errors as a sensitivity, not as a positive-support
model of all possible heights. Its likelihood is not compared with either
single-endpoint likelihood.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-models
#| code-summary: "Show Phase Three fitting and estimand helpers"
p3 <- "outputs/sprouts/phase-three"
p3_compute <- recompute || isTRUE(params$refit_phase_three) || isTRUE(params$bootstrap)
p3_read <- function(name) read.csv(file.path(p3, "tables", paste0(name, ".csv")), check.names = FALSE)
p3_write <- function(x, name) write.csv(x, file.path(p3, "tables", paste0(name, ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)
p3_control <- function(bfgs = FALSE) {
  if (bfgs) glmmTMBControl(optimizer = optim, optArgs = list(method = "BFGS"),
    optCtrl = list(maxit = 10000, reltol = 1e-10), rank_check = "stop") else
    glmmTMBControl(optCtrl = list(iter.max = 3000, eval.max = 5000), rank_check = "stop")
}
p3_start <- function(m) list(beta = unname(fixef(m)$cond),
  betadisp = unname(fixef(m)$disp), theta = unname(glmmTMB::getME(m, "theta")))
p3_fit <- function(id, mean, dispersion, dat, fam, bfgs = FALSE) {
  path <- file.path(p3, "models", paste0(id, ".rds"))
  if (isTRUE(params$refit_phase_three)) {
    message("RD03 Phase Three fitting ", id)
    warnings <- character()
    m <- withCallingHandlers(glmmTMB(mean, dispformula = dispersion, data = dat,
      family = fam, REML = FALSE, na.action = na.fail, control = p3_control(bfgs)),
      warning = function(w) { warnings <<- c(warnings, conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") })
    attr(m, "rd03_warnings") <- paste(unique(warnings), collapse = "; ")
    saveRDS(m, path)
  } else {
    if (!file.exists(path)) stop("Missing Phase Three fit: ", id, "; use explicit refit_phase_three:true.")
    m <- readRDS(path)
  }
  stopifnot(nobs(m) == nrow(dat))
  m
}
p3_record <- function(m, id) {
  v <- VarCorr(m)$cond
  correlations <- unlist(lapply(v, function(z) attr(z, "correlation")[lower.tri(z)]))
  data.frame(model_id = id, fit_status = "fit", n = nobs(m),
    mean = paste(deparse(formula(m)), collapse = " "),
    dispersion = paste(deparse(formula(m, component = "disp")), collapse = " "),
    family = family(m)$family, link = family(m)$link,
    convergence = m$fit$convergence, pd_hessian = isTRUE(m$sdr$pdHess),
    max_gradient = max(abs(m$sdr$gradient.fixed)), AIC = AIC(m),
    min_random_sd = min(unlist(lapply(v, function(z) attr(z, "stddev")))),
    max_absolute_correlation = if (length(correlations)) max(abs(correlations)) else 0,
    warnings = if (is.null(attr(m, "rd03_warnings"))) "" else attr(m, "rd03_warnings"))
}
# This compact predictor is also used inside each bootstrap refit. Every
# log-link prediction integrates the refitted macro variance, not its original value.
p3_values <- function(m, dat, endpoint, coefficients = fixef(m)$cond) {
  sp <- as.character(dat$spp[1])
  visit <- if (endpoint == "increment") c("5", "10") else if (endpoint == "joint") c("1", "5", "10") else "10"
  grid <- expand.grid(site = levels(dat$site), treat = levels(dat$treat), visit = visit,
    KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  for (v in c("site", "treat")) grid[[v]] <- factor(grid[[v]], levels = levels(dat[[v]]))
  if (endpoint == "increment") grid$period <- factor(grid$visit, levels = levels(dat$period))
  if (endpoint == "joint") grid$age <- factor(grid$visit, levels = levels(dat$age))
  X <- model.matrix(delete.response(terms(lme4::nobars(formula(m)))), grid)
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(X), names(fixef(m)$cond)))
  eta <- drop(X %*% coefficients)
  macro_variance <- if (family(m)$link == "log") VarCorr(m)$cond$plot[1, 1] else 0
  grid$value <- family(m)$linkinv(eta) * exp(macro_variance / 2)
  cells <- aggregate(value ~ treat + visit, grid, mean)
  get <- function(tr, age) cells$value[cells$treat == tr & cells$visit == age]
  out <- c()
  for (tr in levels(dat$treat)) {
    if (endpoint != "increment") out[paste0("height:", tr)] <- get(tr, "10")
    if (endpoint != "height") {
      early <- if (endpoint == "joint") (get(tr, "5") - get(tr, "1")) / 4 else get(tr, "5")
      late <- if (endpoint == "joint") (get(tr, "10") - get(tr, "5")) / 5 else get(tr, "10")
      out[paste0("early:", tr)] <- early
      out[paste0("late:", tr)] <- late
      out[paste0("change:", tr)] <- late - early
    }
  }
  for (tr in c("GS", "HA")) {
    if (endpoint != "increment") out[paste0("height_contrast:", tr, "-HD")] <-
      unname(out[paste0("height:", tr)] - out["height:HD"])
    if (endpoint != "height") out[paste0("change_contrast:", tr, "-HD")] <-
      unname(out[paste0("change:", tr)] - out["change:HD"])
  }
  out
}
```

We fit the planned numerical and covariance sensitivities on identical species
rows. The compact predictor must reproduce Phase Two's independently checked
arithmetic predictions before it is used for simulation. For the joint-height
model, linear contrasts retain the covariance of all three visits when deriving
both interval rates and their difference.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-fits
if (p3_compute) {
  for (folder in c("models", "tables", "figures", "simulations"))
    dir.create(file.path(p3, folder), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  p3_wide <- readRDS(file.path(input, "measurements.rds"))
  p3_inc <- bind_rows(mutate(p3_wide, period = "5", ht_inc = ht_inc5),
    mutate(p3_wide, period = "10", ht_inc = ht_inc10)) |>
    mutate(period = factor(period, levels = c("5", "10")))
  p3_models <- list(); p3_data <- list(); p3_records <- list(); sensitivity <- list(); omits <- list()
  joint_results <- list()
  for (sp in levels(p3_wide$spp)) {
    h <- droplevels(filter(p3_wide, spp == sp))
    ii <- droplevels(filter(p3_inc, spp == sp))
    for (endpoint in c("height", "increment")) {
      id <- if (endpoint == "height") paste0("h_", sp) else paste0("i_", sp, "_macro")
      path <- file.path(p2, "models", paste0(id, ".rds"))
      if (!file.exists(path)) stop("Missing prerequisite: ", path)
      m <- readRDS(path)
      stopifnot(rd_usable(m))
      dat <- if (endpoint == "height") h else ii
      p3_models[[id]] <- m; p3_data[[id]] <- dat
      # Reconcile the bootstrap predictor with Phase Two's independently
      # checked fixed-effect design and analytic macro integration.
      reference <- rd_means(m, dat, endpoint, id)$table
      compact <- p3_values(m, dat, endpoint)
      keys <- if (endpoint == "height") paste0("height:", reference$treat) else
        paste0(ifelse(reference$period == "5", "early:", "late:"), reference$treat)
      stopifnot(max(abs(reference$estimate - compact[keys])) < 1e-8)
      alt_id <- paste0(id, "_bfgs")
      alt <- p3_fit(alt_id, formula(m), formula(m, component = "disp"), dat, family(m), TRUE)
      p3_records[[alt_id]] <- p3_record(alt, alt_id)
      sensitivity[[alt_id]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, comparison = alt_id,
        usable = rd_usable(alt), objective_difference = abs(m$fit$objective - alt$fit$objective),
        max_estimand_difference = if (rd_usable(alt)) max(abs(p3_values(m, dat, endpoint) - p3_values(alt, dat, endpoint))) else NA_real_)
    }
    diag_id <- paste0("i_", sp, "_macro_diagonal")
    md <- p3_fit(diag_id, ht_inc ~ treat * period + site + diag(0 + period | plot) + (1 | tree),
      ~treat * period, ii, gaussian())
    p3_records[[diag_id]] <- p3_record(md, diag_id)
    for (site in levels(ii$site)) {
      dd <- droplevels(filter(ii, .data$site != .env$site))
      for (shape in c("correlated", "diagonal")) {
        id <- paste0("i_", sp, "_", shape, "_omit_", match(site, levels(ii$site)))
        base <- if (shape == "correlated") p3_models[[paste0("i_", sp, "_macro")]] else md
        mm <- p3_fit(id, formula(base), formula(base, component = "disp"), dd, family(base), TRUE)
        p3_records[[id]] <- p3_record(mm, id)
        if (rd_usable(mm)) omits[[id]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, spp = sp,
          omitted_site = site, estimand = names(p3_values(mm, dd, "increment")),
          value = unname(p3_values(mm, dd, "increment")))
      }
    }
    hh <- h |> pivot_longer(c(ht1, ht5, ht10), names_to = "age", values_to = "height") |>
      mutate(age = factor(sub("ht", "", age), levels = c("1", "5", "10")))
    jid <- paste0("joint_", sp)
    ju <- p3_fit(paste0(jid, "_unstructured"), height ~ treat * age + site * age + us(0 + age | plot) + us(0 + age | tree),
      ~0, hh, gaussian())
    jua <- p3_fit(paste0(jid, "_unstructured_bfgs"), formula(ju), ~0, hh, gaussian(), TRUE)
    p3_records[[paste0(jid, "_unstructured")]] <- p3_record(ju, paste0(jid, "_unstructured"))
    p3_records[[paste0(jid, "_unstructured_bfgs")]] <- p3_record(jua, paste0(jid, "_unstructured_bfgs"))
    jm <- p3_fit(jid, height ~ treat * age + site * age + rr(0 + age | plot, d = 2) + us(0 + age | tree),
      ~0, hh, gaussian())
    ja <- p3_fit(paste0(jid, "_bfgs"), formula(jm), ~0, hh, gaussian(), TRUE)
    p3_records[[jid]] <- p3_record(jm, jid)
    p3_records[[paste0(jid, "_bfgs")]] <- p3_record(ja, paste0(jid, "_bfgs"))
    # BFGS must pass the same convergence/Hessian check as every other fit.
    # Objective agreement does not erase a failed nlminb convergence flag.
    stopifnot(rd_usable(ja), abs(jm$fit$objective - ja$fit$objective) < 1e-4)
    jv <- p3_values(ja, hh, "joint")
    direct <- predict(ja, newdata = hh, re.form = NA)
    stopifnot(all(is.finite(direct)))
    direct_cells <- mutate(hh, fitted_height = as.numeric(direct)) |>
      group_by(site, treat, age) |> summarise(value = mean(fitted_height), .groups = "drop") |>
      group_by(treat, age) |> summarise(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop")
    for (tr in levels(hh$treat)) {
      get_height <- function(a) direct_cells$value[direct_cells$treat == tr & direct_cells$age == a]
      early <- (get_height("5") - get_height("1")) / 4
      late <- (get_height("10") - get_height("5")) / 5
      stopifnot(abs(jv[paste0("height:", tr)] - get_height("10")) < 1e-8,
        abs(jv[paste0("early:", tr)] - early) < 1e-8,
        abs(jv[paste0("late:", tr)] - late) < 1e-8,
        abs(jv[paste0("change:", tr)] - (late - early)) < 1e-8)
    }
    sensitivity[[jid]] <- data.frame(model_id = jid, comparison = paste0(jid, "_bfgs"),
      usable = rd_usable(ja), objective_difference = abs(jm$fit$objective - ja$fit$objective),
      max_estimand_difference = max(abs(jv - p3_values(jm, hh, "joint"))))
    hv <- p3_values(p3_models[[paste0("h_", sp)]], h, "height")
    iv <- p3_values(p3_models[[paste0("i_", sp, "_macro")]], ii, "increment")
    # Identity-link estimands are linear in the mean coefficients. Applying
    # the same derivation to each basis vector retains covariance of shared H5.
    basis <- diag(length(fixef(ja)$cond))
    J <- vapply(seq_len(ncol(basis)), function(k)
      p3_values(ja, hh, "joint", coefficients = basis[, k]), numeric(length(jv)))
    joint_se <- sqrt(diag(J %*% as.matrix(vcov(ja)$cond) %*% t(J)))
    joint_results[[sp]] <- data.frame(spp = sp, estimand = names(jv), joint_value = unname(jv),
      joint_se = joint_se, joint_lcl = jv - qnorm(.975) * joint_se,
      joint_ucl = jv + qnorm(.975) * joint_se,
      endpoint_value = unname(c(hv, iv)[names(jv)]),
      uncertainty = "provisional joint-height Wald; covariance model conditional")
  }
  p3_write(bind_rows(p3_records), "rd03-fit-register")
  p3_write(bind_rows(sensitivity), "optimizer-checks")
  p3_write(bind_rows(omits), "site-omission-estimands")
  p3_write(bind_rows(joint_results), "joint-height-sensitivity")
}
knitr::kable(p3_read("rd03-fit-register") |>
  select(model_id, convergence, pd_hessian, max_gradient, min_random_sd, max_absolute_correlation), digits = 5)
```

The optimizer comparison separates agreement on the complete cohort from
instability after reducing the experiment to three sites. The joint-height
table compares the same arithmetic estimands; differences reflect its distinct
mean and covariance assumptions, including age-specific site effects.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-sensitivity-review
knitr::kable(p3_read("optimizer-checks"), digits = 6)
knitr::kable(p3_read("joint-height-sensitivity") |>
  select(spp, estimand, joint_value, joint_lcl, joint_ucl, endpoint_value), digits = 4)
```

We retain the successfully fitted site-omission treatment contrasts below;
their point estimates diagnose influence, while the fit register identifies
omissions that supply no usable estimates. These are comparisons among the
remaining three observed sites, not additional independent experiments.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-site-review
knitr::kable(p3_read("site-omission-estimands") |>
  filter(grepl("_contrast:", estimand)), digits = 4)
```

The complete-cohort endpoint models agree under both optimizers. Setting macro
period covariance to zero raises AIC by 8.40 for tanoak and 8.28 for redwood on
the same rows, with little change in point estimates and wider provisional
change intervals. We therefore retain the correlated macro-period models and
keep the diagonal specification as a sensitivity. Both retain variation among
macros in growth-rate change; neither deletes the experimental clustering.

BFGS recovers the three Phase Two failed omissions, but redwood's Camp Six and
Waldo South omissions lie at almost perfect macro-period correlation. Tanoak's
Camp Six omission has correlation 0.9997 and a relatively large gradient; two
other tanoak BFGS omissions have nonpositive Hessians even though their Phase
Two nlminb fits were usable. Diagonal omissions also encounter zero variances
and failed Hessians. This is weakly estimated covariance in small subsets, not
a reason to discard sites or claim that one simpler covariance solves inference.
Across the four usable correlated redwood omissions, the GS–HD difference in
slowing ranges from -0.089 to +0.015 m/year. The HA–HD difference ranges from
+0.024 to +0.099 m/year, without establishing precision for that comparison.
Thus even the sign of the GS–HD temporal comparison depends on which sites
remain, whereas the Phase Two height comparison retained a positive GS–HD sign.

The unrestricted joint-height macro covariance is numerically singular for
both species. Rank-two macro fits have usable BFGS Hessians and agree closely
in objective with nlminb, whose false-convergence flags remain recorded. We use
the BFGS fits only as sensitivities. Their redwood GS–HD year-10 contrast is
4.56 m, versus 4.65 m from the endpoint model; the HA–HD contrast is 0.97 versus
0.96 m. Redwood change estimates differ by at most 0.004 m/year, and tanoak
change estimates by less than 0.001 m/year. Their uncertainty is less stable:
the joint model's provisional tanoak change intervals exclude zero in GS, LD,
and HA, unlike the endpoint model's Phase Two intervals. The joint clump
covariance pools across treatments and site blocking is age-specific, so this
is a different set of covariance assumptions, not independent confirmation
of slowing. Differential-change intervals still span zero for both species.

### Simulated support and refitted bootstrap

We inspect 500 simulated datasets from each separate year-10 model, keeping
Gaussian draws below zero in the diagnostic count. A log link guarantees a
positive mean, not positive observations. We retain these models provisionally
because the Phase Two Gamma alternative had poorer fit and detectable residual
misfit; this is a consequential approximation, not evidence that negative
heights are biologically possible. A lognormal model would be an additional
distributional change and is not needed solely to erase a small simulation tail.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-height-diagnostics
if (p3_compute) {
  diagnostics <- list()
  for (j in seq_along(p3_models)) {
    id <- names(p3_models)[j]; m <- p3_models[[j]]
    set.seed(20261115 + j)
    sim <- simulate(m, nsim = 500)
    dh <- DHARMa::createDHARMa(simulatedResponse = as.matrix(sim),
      observedResponse = model.response(model.frame(m)), fittedPredictedResponse = rowMeans(as.matrix(sim)),
      integerResponse = FALSE, seed = 20261115 + j)
    diagnostics[[id]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, simulations = 500, seed = 20261115 + j,
      simulated_nonpositive_fraction = mean(as.matrix(sim) <= 0),
      uniformity_p = DHARMa::testUniformity(dh, plot = FALSE)$p.value,
      dispersion_p = DHARMa::testDispersion(dh, plot = FALSE)$p.value)
  }
  p3_write(bind_rows(diagnostics), "simulation-diagnostics")
  joint_support <- list()
  for (j in seq_along(levels(p3_wide$spp))) {
    sp <- levels(p3_wide$spp)[j]
    jm <- readRDS(file.path(p3, "models", paste0("joint_", sp, "_bfgs.rds")))
    set.seed(20261120 + j)
    js <- as.matrix(simulate(jm, nsim = 500))
    age <- model.frame(jm)$age
    joint_support[[sp]] <- bind_rows(lapply(levels(age), function(a)
      data.frame(spp = sp, age = a, simulations = 500, seed = 20261120 + j,
        simulated_nonpositive_fraction = mean(js[age == a, , drop = FALSE] <= 0))))
  }
  p3_write(bind_rows(joint_support), "joint-simulation-support")
}
knitr::kable(p3_read("simulation-diagnostics"), digits = 5)
knitr::kable(p3_read("joint-simulation-support"), digits = 5)
```

The separate year-10 models generate about 1.4 nonpositive tanoak heights and
7.8 nonpositive redwood heights per 1,000 simulated observations. Their
simulation uniformity and dispersion checks give no strong evidence of
misfit, although that does not validate the Gaussian lower tail. The joint
Gaussian identity sensitivity is less suitable as a full height distribution:
about 5.0% of simulated year-1 tanoak heights and 3.8% of redwood heights are
nonpositive. Together with its covariance boundaries and pooled clump
covariance, that supports retaining it as a sensitivity rather than replacing
the endpoint models or using its narrower tanoak intervals as accepted evidence.

We predeclare **2,000 simulated datasets per selected model** and seed
**20261116**. Simulation preserves the original rows, four observed site blocks,
16 macros, repeated clumps, and fitted dispersion. Separate species simulations
support within-species comparisons only. Every refit integrates its own macro
variance for log-link arithmetic means. Original fitted coefficients supply
starting values, allowing valid Gaussian simulations containing negative
observations to be fitted with the log mean link. We try nlminb first and BFGS
after any error, nonzero convergence code, or nonpositive Hessian. Both attempts
and their warnings remain recorded. We do not replace failed datasets or
silently treat their estimates as usable.

The bootstrap uses basic pointwise 95% intervals, reflecting the distribution of refitted
estimate minus original estimate. These intervals propagate variance estimation
under the selected model, but are conditional on the model and on successful
refits. We show the approximate centered-bootstrap two-sided tail probabilities
for the four reserved redwood contrasts and their Holm adjustment. These are
model-based sensitivity tests, not randomization tests or a demonstration of
nominal coverage with four sites. Other comparisons remain exploratory. The
Monte Carlo table reports binomial order-statistic uncertainty in each interval
endpoint and the intervals from the first and second 1,000 simulations; it
assesses simulation precision, not robustness to model misspecification.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-bootstrap
#| code-summary: "Show 2,000-refit bootstrap and interval calculations"
p3_boot_one <- function(job, models, datasets, values_fun, start_fun, control_fun) {
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(glmmTMB))
  id <- job$id; m <- models[[id]]; dat <- datasets[[id]]
  endpoint <- if (startsWith(id, "h_")) "height" else "increment"
  set.seed(job$seed)
  dat[[all.vars(formula(m))[1]]] <- simulate(m, nsim = 1)[[1]]
  warning_text <- character(); error_text <- ""; attempts <- list(); chosen <- NULL
  for (attempt in 1:2) {
    warning_text <- character(); error_text <- ""
    mm <- tryCatch(withCallingHandlers(glmmTMB(formula(m),
      dispformula = formula(m, component = "disp"), family = family(m), data = dat,
      REML = FALSE, na.action = na.fail, start = start_fun(m), control = control_fun(attempt == 2)),
      warning = function(w) { warning_text <<- c(warning_text, conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") }),
      error = function(e) { error_text <<- conditionMessage(e); NULL })
    usable <- !is.null(mm) && mm$fit$convergence == 0 && isTRUE(mm$sdr$pdHess)
    v <- if (!is.null(mm)) VarCorr(mm)$cond else list()
    sd <- unlist(lapply(v, function(z) attr(z, "stddev")))
    cor <- unlist(lapply(v, function(z) attr(z, "correlation")[lower.tri(z)]))
    attempts[[attempt]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, replicate = job$b, seed = job$seed,
      attempt = attempt, usable = usable,
      convergence = if (is.null(mm)) NA_integer_ else mm$fit$convergence,
      pd_hessian = !is.null(mm) && isTRUE(mm$sdr$pdHess),
      max_gradient = if (is.null(mm)) NA_real_ else max(abs(mm$sdr$gradient.fixed)),
      min_random_sd = if (length(sd)) min(sd) else NA_real_,
      max_absolute_correlation = if (length(cor)) max(abs(cor)) else 0,
      boundary = any(sd < 1e-4) || any(abs(cor) > .999),
      warnings = paste(unique(warning_text), collapse = "; "), error = error_text)
    if (usable) { chosen <- mm; break }
  }
  list(attempts = do.call(rbind, attempts),
    values = if (is.null(chosen)) NULL else values_fun(chosen, dat, endpoint))
}
```

We distribute independent simulations across local R workers, using seeds
generated before scheduling so worker count cannot change a dataset. Failed
connections stop startup; the completed bootstrap is saved as an ignored
computational object for later summary regeneration.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-bootstrap-run
if (p3_compute) {
  bootstrap_path <- file.path(p3, "simulations", "bootstrap.rds")
  if (isTRUE(params$bootstrap)) {
    # Master-generated seeds make results independent of worker count and scheduling.
    set.seed(20261116)
    jobs <- unlist(lapply(names(p3_models), function(id) lapply(seq_len(2000),
      function(b) list(id = id, b = b, seed = sample.int(.Machine$integer.max, 1)))), recursive = FALSE)
    workers <- min(8L, max(1L, parallel::detectCores() - 2L))
    cl <- parallel::makePSOCKcluster(workers, setup_timeout = 30)
    boot <- tryCatch({
      parallel::clusterEvalQ(cl, { source(".Rprofile"); library(glmmTMB); NULL })
      # Batches retain progress without retaining comparison snapshots.
      ans <- vector("list", length(jobs))
      for (first in seq(1L, length(jobs), by = 200L)) {
        ix <- first:min(first + 199L, length(jobs))
        ans[ix] <- parallel::parLapplyLB(cl, jobs[ix], p3_boot_one,
          models = p3_models, datasets = p3_data, values_fun = p3_values,
          start_fun = p3_start, control_fun = p3_control)
        message("RD03 bootstrap: ", max(ix), " / ", length(jobs), " datasets")
      }
      ans
    }, finally = parallel::stopCluster(cl))
    saveRDS(boot, bootstrap_path)
  } else {
    if (!file.exists(bootstrap_path)) stop("Missing Phase Three bootstrap; explicit bootstrap:true is required.")
    boot <- readRDS(bootstrap_path)
  }
}
```

We summarize every attempted dataset and use only refits meeting the unchanged
convergence and Hessian criteria for intervals. Comparing refitted standard
errors with the earlier Wald errors shows the effect of propagating fitted
variance uncertainty under these models; Monte Carlo endpoint bands show how
precisely 2,000 simulations locate the reported limits.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-bootstrap-summary
if (p3_compute) {
  attempts <- bind_rows(lapply(boot, `[[`, "attempts"))
  p3_write(attempts, "bootstrap-refits")
  summary_rows <- list(); intervals <- list(); stability <- list(); gradient_sensitivity <- list()
  for (id in names(p3_models)) {
    subset <- boot[vapply(boot, function(z) z$attempts$model_id[1] == id, logical(1))]
    stopifnot(length(subset) == 2000L)
    ok <- vapply(subset, function(z) !is.null(z$values), logical(1))
    last <- attempts |> filter(model_id == id) |> group_by(replicate) |> slice_tail(n = 1) |> ungroup()
    summary_rows[[id]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, seed = 20261116, requested = 2000,
      successful = sum(ok), failed = sum(!ok), retried = sum(last$attempt == 2),
      successful_boundary = sum(last$usable & last$boundary),
      successful_gradient_above_0_01 = sum(last$usable & last$max_gradient > .01, na.rm = TRUE),
      max_successful_gradient = max(last$max_gradient[last$usable]),
      first_half_successful = sum(ok[1:1000]), second_half_successful = sum(ok[1001:2000]))
    m <- p3_models[[id]]; dat <- p3_data[[id]]
    point <- p3_values(m, dat, if (startsWith(id, "h_")) "height" else "increment")
    draws <- do.call(rbind, lapply(subset[ok], `[[`, "values"))
    stopifnot(nrow(draws) > 1000L, identical(colnames(draws), names(point)), all(is.finite(draws)))
    # A scale-dependent gradient screen is a numerical sensitivity, not a
    # replacement for convergence/Hessian criteria or a coverage guarantee.
    gradient <- last$max_gradient[match(which(ok), last$replicate)]
    strict <- is.finite(gradient) & gradient <= .01
    stopifnot(sum(strict) > 1000L)
    for (j in seq_along(point)) {
      x <- draws[, j]; n <- length(x); q <- quantile(x, c(.025, .975), names = FALSE)
      intervals[[paste(id, j)]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, spp = as.character(dat$spp[1]),
        estimand = names(point)[j], estimate = unname(point[j]), se = sd(x),
        lcl = 2 * unname(point[j]) - q[2], ucl = 2 * unname(point[j]) - q[1],
        bootstrap_bias = mean(x) - unname(point[j]), successful = n,
        p_centered = (1 + sum(abs(x - point[j]) >= abs(point[j]))) / (n + 1),
        uncertainty = "basic 95% parametric bootstrap; successful refits; model conditional")
      sq <- quantile(x[strict], c(.025, .975), names = FALSE)
      gradient_sensitivity[[paste(id, j)]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, spp = as.character(dat$spp[1]),
        estimand = names(point)[j], estimate = unname(point[j]), gradient_cutoff = .01,
        retained = sum(strict), excluded_successful = sum(!strict),
        lcl = 2 * unname(point[j]) - sq[2], ucl = 2 * unname(point[j]) - sq[1],
        uncertainty = "basic 95% bootstrap; convergence/Hessian pass and max gradient <= 0.01; numerical sensitivity")
      for (prob in c(.025, .975)) {
        ranks <- pmax(1L, pmin(n, qbinom(c(.025, .975), n, prob) + 1L))
        sx <- sort(x)
        half_q <- vapply(list(1:1000, 1001:2000), function(ix) {
          vals <- vapply(subset[ix][ok[ix]], function(z) z$values[j], numeric(1))
          2 * point[j] - quantile(vals, prob, names = FALSE)
        }, numeric(1))
        stability[[paste(id, j, prob)]] <- data.frame(model_id = id, estimand = names(point)[j],
          endpoint = if (prob == .975) "lower" else "upper",
          endpoint_value = 2 * unname(point[j]) - quantile(x, prob, names = FALSE),
          mc_low = 2 * unname(point[j]) - sx[ranks[2]], mc_high = 2 * unname(point[j]) - sx[ranks[1]],
          first_1000 = half_q[1], second_1000 = half_q[2])
      }
    }
  }
  estimates <- bind_rows(intervals)
  wald_means <- p2_read("candidate-means") |>
    mutate(estimand = paste0(ifelse(period == "year10", "height", ifelse(period == "5", "early", "late")), ":", treat))
  wald_contrasts <- p2_read("candidate-contrasts") |>
    mutate(estimand = case_when(
      grepl(" height$", contrast) ~ paste0("height_contrast:", sub(" minus HD height", "-HD", contrast)),
      grepl(" period change$", contrast) ~ paste0("change_contrast:", sub(" minus HD period change", "-HD", contrast)),
      TRUE ~ paste0("change:", sub(" later minus earlier", "", contrast))))
  wald <- bind_rows(wald_means, wald_contrasts) |>
    select(model_id, spp, estimand, wald_estimate = estimate, wald_se = se, wald_lcl = lcl, wald_ucl = ucl)
  estimates <- left_join(estimates, wald, by = c("model_id", "spp", "estimand")) |>
    mutate(bootstrap_to_wald_se = se / wald_se)
  stopifnot(!anyNA(estimates$wald_se), max(abs(estimates$estimate - estimates$wald_estimate)) < 1e-8)
  confirmatory <- estimates |> filter(spp == "SESE", grepl("_contrast:", estimand)) |>
    mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p_centered, method = "holm"),
      interpretation = "approximate model-based sensitivity; four-contrast family")
  stopifnot(nrow(confirmatory) == 4L)
  p3_write(bind_rows(summary_rows), "bootstrap-summary")
  p3_write(estimates, "bootstrap-estimates")
  p3_write(confirmatory, "redwood-planned-contrasts")
  p3_write(bind_rows(stability), "monte-carlo-stability")
  p3_write(bind_rows(gradient_sensitivity), "gradient-sensitivity")
  writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), file.path(p3, "tables", "session-info.txt"))
}
knitr::kable(p3_read("bootstrap-summary") |>
  select(model_id, requested, successful, failed, retried,
    successful_boundary, successful_gradient_above_0_01),
  col.names = c("Model", "Requested", "Successful", "Failed", "Retried", "Boundary", "Gradient >0.01"))
```

Both height models yielded 2,000 usable refits. Tanoak increments yielded 1,992
and redwood increments 1,895, leaving 8 (0.4%) and 105 (5.25%) failed datasets,
respectively. The second optimizer was needed for 1,304 tanoak and 1,580 redwood
datasets. Among successful increment refits, 1,223 tanoak and 1,434 redwood fits
met the declared boundary flag (random SD below 0.0001 or absolute correlation
above 0.999). Height-model boundary counts were 41 for tanoak and 183 for
redwood. These are properties of the simulated fits, not evidence of additional
independent replication. In particular, frequent temporal boundaries and
conditioning on successful refits limit any claim of calibrated coverage.

Large gradients can remain after a convergence code of zero and a positive
Hessian. The additional numerical sensitivity below restricts successful draws
to maximum absolute gradient at most 0.01. This cutoff depends on parameter
scales; it diagnoses sensitivity rather than certifying accuracy. We retain
the original intervals and all attempt records, and do not reclassify discarded
draws as additional successful simulations.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-gradient-review
knitr::kable(p3_read("gradient-sensitivity") |>
  filter(grepl("^(change:|.*_contrast:)", estimand)) |>
  select(model_id, estimand, retained, excluded_successful, estimate, lcl, ucl), digits = 4)
```

The gradient screen retains all height refits, 1,473 tanoak increment refits,
and 1,878 redwood increment refits. Its interval endpoints differ from the
original increment intervals by at most 0.0036 and 0.0014 m/year, respectively,
without changing which change intervals span zero. This is reassuring about
these numerical endpoints, but does not resolve covariance misspecification
or the instability of estimating variance components from four blocks.

These treatment contrasts use the same four-site arithmetic target as the
point estimates. Holm adjustment applies to the two height and two differential
change contrasts together; a cell-wise change interval is not a test that
slowing differs between treatments.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-contrast-review
knitr::kable(p3_read("redwood-planned-contrasts") |>
  select(estimand, estimate, lcl, ucl, p_centered, p_holm), digits = 4)
```

For redwood, GS–HD year-10 height is 4.65 m (basic 95% interval 2.58–6.54 m),
with approximate centered-bootstrap probability 0.00050 and Holm-adjusted
probability 0.0020. HA–HD height is 0.96 m (-0.70–2.51 m). Differences in
later-minus-earlier rates are -0.039 m/year for GS–HD (-0.143–0.071) and
+0.056 m/year for HA–HD (-0.057–0.173); the latter three adjusted probabilities
are all about 0.72. These model-based calculations support the stronger
attained-height contrast without establishing an arrangement advantage,
treatment-specific slowing, or temporal equivalence.

For the reserved redwood contrasts, the next table compares the first and
second halves of the simulation and gives order-statistic uncertainty in each
full-sample interval endpoint. The complete machine-readable table includes
every treatment mean and temporal estimand.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-monte-carlo-review
knitr::kable(p3_read("monte-carlo-stability") |>
  filter(grepl("SESE", model_id), grepl("_contrast:", estimand)), digits = 4)
```

For the four reserved redwood contrasts, first-half versus second-half interval
endpoints differ by at most 0.131 m for height and 0.0079 m/year for temporal
change. The GS–HD height lower endpoint is 2.58 m, with an order-statistic
Monte Carlo band of 2.43–2.65 m. The temporal contrast endpoints have Monte Carlo
bands about 0.011–0.017 m/year wide. Simulation precision does not change the
qualitative contrast interpretation, but the extra decimals in the saved
tables should not be read as biological precision. Bootstrap standard errors
are close to the provisional Wald errors under the chosen models; that
agreement does not establish finite-sample coverage.

The interval-specific rates remain available without averaging away their
different durations. The ratio of bootstrap to provisional Wald standard error
shows how refitting changes the earlier uncertainty calculation under the
chosen model; it does not establish that either interval has exact coverage.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-interval-review
knitr::kable(p3_read("bootstrap-estimates") |>
  filter(grepl("^(early|late):", estimand)) |>
  select(spp, estimand, estimate, lcl, ucl, bootstrap_to_wald_se), digits = 4)
```

### Proposed size display and supplementary temporal detail

We show year-10 height as the main display proposal and retain treatment-wise
changes in growth rate as supplementary detail. A temporal panel in the main
figure would invite a strong treatment-specific interpretation that needs
support from the differential-change contrasts. Points and intervals use the
refitted bootstrap, with redwood first and tanoak providing context.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-display
if (p3_compute) {
  display <- p3_read("bootstrap-estimates") |>
    filter(grepl("^(height|change):", estimand)) |>
    mutate(treat = factor(sub(".*:", "", estimand), levels = c("GS", "LD", "HA", "HD")),
      species = factor(spp, levels = c("SESE", "LIDE"), labels = c("Redwood", "Tanoak")))
  p3_write(display, "proposed-display")
  for (kind in c("height", "change")) {
    z <- filter(display, grepl(paste0("^", kind, ":"), estimand))
    g <- ggplot(z, aes(treat, estimate)) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey80", linewidth = .35) +
      geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl), width = .12, linewidth = .6) +
      geom_point(size = 2.7, colour = "#22665D") + facet_wrap(~species) +
      labs(x = "Overstory treatment", y = if (kind == "height") "Year-10 tallest-clump height (m)" else
        "Later minus earlier annual height change (m/year)") +
      theme_bw(base_size = 12) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
    ggsave(file.path(p3, "figures", paste0("proposed-", kind, ".png")), g, width = 8, height = 4.3, dpi = 180)
  }
}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(p3, "figures", "proposed-height.png"))
```

**Proposed main caption.** Arithmetic mean year-10 height of the tallest sprout
on each recorded clump under GS, LD, HA, and HD, shown separately for redwood and
tanoak. Predictions average the four observed sites equally and integrate the
fitted Gaussian macro effect in separate Gaussian(log) models. Bars are basic
pointwise 95% parametric-bootstrap intervals from successful refits among 2,000 simulated
datasets per model. They are model conditional and exclude uncertainty about
model selection and clump inclusion. The tallest stem can change between visits;
these are selected-cohort height estimates, not stand-wide productivity or
survival estimates. The display awaits acceptance.

The supplemental temporal display keeps the two unequal intervals explicit:
the plotted quantity is $(H_{10}-H_5)/5-(H_5-H_1)/4$. Negative values indicate
a lower later rate of change in clump maximum height, without identifying
the growth history of one stem.

```{r}
#| label: rd03-phase-three-temporal-display
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(p3, "figures", "proposed-change.png"))
```

**Proposed supplementary caption.** Change in annualized tallest-clump height
increment from years 1–5 to years 5–10, standardized equally over the four
observed sites. Separate Gaussian models retain correlated macro-period effects,
a clump intercept, and treatment-by-period residual dispersion. Points are
later minus earlier rates; bars are basic pointwise 95% parametric-bootstrap
intervals conditional on successful refits and the chosen model. Individual
treatment intervals do not test differences in slowing between treatments.
Covariance boundaries and alternative joint-height assumptions limit inference.

### Phase Three conclusion and acceptance handoff

For the display proposal, we select `h_SESE` and `h_LIDE` for attained year-10
height and retain `i_SESE_macro` and `i_LIDE_macro` for supplementary temporal
detail. Redwood GS clumps are clearly taller than HD clumps under the fitted
model, while HA–HD height and differences among treatments in slowing remain
uncertain. Redwood slowing intervals exclude zero in GS, LD, and HD, but not
HA; tanoak's four intervals span zero. Those within-treatment results do not
test differential slowing and remain conditional on the selected covariance.

The joint-height sensitivity supports the point-estimate story while exposing
uncertainty and support limitations. The refitted bootstrap propagates fitted
variance uncertainty, records failed and boundary fits, and locates the
reported endpoints sufficiently well for this display decision. It does not
remove the limitations of four sites, selected clumps, Gaussian support, or
model selection. The main height figure and supplementary temporal figure are
ready for human acceptance; RT02, M02, and D02 remain queued until then. No
manuscript model, claim, or publication display is accepted by this analysis.
